title: Lamentations 3:48–66
context: The voice returns to “I.” The afflicted man weeps without ceasing for the destruction of the daughter of his people, until the LORD looks down from heaven (3:48–51). He recalls being hunted like a bird by enemies without cause, his life cut off in the dungeon, waters over his head, and his own cry that he was cut off (3:52–54). Many readers hear echoes of Jeremiah’s imprisonment in the cistern (Jeremiah 38:6), though the imagery is also common to the psalms of lament (compare Psalm 69:1–2; 88:6) and need not be biographical. He then remembers that the LORD heard his voice, came near, and said “Don’t be afraid,” pleading his cause and redeeming his life (3:55–58). Readers differ on whether 3:56–61 recalls an earlier deliverance or speaks with confident anticipation; on either reading it grounds the prayer that follows. The poem closes with a plea for justice against his enemies (3:59–66), asking the LORD to repay them according to the work of their hands, to give them hardness of heart and his curse, and to pursue them in anger. Both traditions read these lines as an appeal that leaves vengeance with God (compare Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19) rather than a license for personal revenge, and both read them alongside the New Testament call to love and pray for enemies (Matthew 5:44). Their difference over divine hardening (3:65) is treated at Exodus 4:21 and Joshua 11:20 and is not restated here.

verses.text: My eye runs down with streams of water, for the destruction of the daughter of my people.
verses.arminianNotes: The afflicted man’s voice returns: “My eye runs down with streams of water, for the destruction of the daughter of my people” (compare 1:16; 2:11; Jeremiah 14:17). Arminian readers see the compassion of one who weeps with and for his people, an intercession that shares the suffering rather than standing above it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see tears as the fitting response of the godly to God’s judgment on his people, grief that is love rather than rebellion, and many hear in it a foreshadowing of Christ weeping over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Shared ground: both traditions honor tears as part of faith and refuse to shame the grieving.

verses.text: My eye pours down and doesn’t cease, without any intermission,
verses.arminianNotes: “My eye pours down and doesn’t cease, without any intermission.” Arminian readers note the persistence of grief and see in it a longing that keeps reaching toward God, since the tears are tied to the expectation that the LORD will look down (3:50).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see unceasing tears as a form of prayer that waits on God’s sovereign timing, and they note that the man does not stop until the LORD acts. Shared ground: both traditions recognize that grief can last long, and both counsel patience with those who mourn rather than haste to move them on.

verses.text: until the LORD looks down, and sees from heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: The tears continue “until the LORD looks down, and sees from heaven.” Arminian readers hear confidence that God responds to his people’s cry and that the man’s waiting is not in vain, since the LORD attends to the afflicted (compare Psalm 102:19–20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the man’s hope fixed on God’s initiative: deliverance begins when the LORD looks and sees, not when the sufferer achieves it. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as faith waiting for God to act, and both hear in it Zion’s repeated plea that the LORD look and see (1:11; 2:20).

verses.text: My eye affects my soul, because of all the daughters of my city.
verses.arminianNotes: “My eye affects my soul, because of all the daughters of my city.” Arminian readers see grief entering the man’s inmost being as he sees what has befallen the people of his city, and they hear in it the costly compassion of one who will not look away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the man’s sorrow as godly grief that shares the pain of God’s people and brings it before him. Whether “daughters” means the women of Jerusalem or, as some read it, its surrounding towns, the grief embraces the whole community. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as compassion, not detachment.

verses.text: They have chased me relentlessly like a bird, those who are my enemies without cause.
verses.arminianNotes: “They have chased me relentlessly like a bird, those who are my enemies without cause.” Arminian readers note the man’s claim of innocence toward these enemies alongside the community’s confession of sin to God (3:42), and they see both as true at different levels.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same distinction: guilt before God does not justify enemies who hunt without cause, and the sufferer may appeal to God against them (compare Psalm 35:7; 69:4). Shared ground: both traditions hold together confession toward God and a claim of wrongful treatment by others.

verses.text: They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and have cast a stone on me.
verses.arminianNotes: “They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and have cast a stone on me.” Many readers hear an echo of Jeremiah lowered into a cistern (Jeremiah 38:6), though the image also fits the lament tradition’s pit of death; Arminian readers stress the real injustice done by human enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pit as the place of near-death from which God alone rescues (compare Psalm 40:2), and they read the stone as sealing the man’s hopelessness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an experience of being left for dead, whether biographical or representative, and neither presses the details beyond the poem.

verses.text: Waters flowed over my head. I said, “I am cut off.”
verses.arminianNotes: Waters flow over the man’s head and he says that he is cut off (compare Psalm 69:1–2; Jonah 2:3–5). Arminian readers hear the depth of despair, and they note that on most readings the cry is recalled in light of the answered prayer that follows (3:55–57), so it is not the last word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the overwhelming waters as an image of judgment and death that only God can reverse, and they stress that the man’s sense of being cut off did not cancel God’s hold on him. Shared ground: both traditions treat the feeling of being cut off with pastoral seriousness and hold out the hope the following verses voice.

verses.text: I called on your name, LORD, out of the lowest dungeon.
verses.arminianNotes: “I called on your name, LORD, out of the lowest dungeon.” Arminian readers see the turning point in the man’s response: from the depths he calls on God, and they read this as faith expressed when every other help is gone, a call God welcomes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see calling on the LORD’s name as the cry of faith God himself sustains, and they note that the depth of the dungeon highlights the greatness of his rescue (compare Psalm 130:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as prayer from the depths that is heard by God.

verses.text: You heard my voice: “Don’t hide your ear from my sighing, and my cry.”
verses.arminianNotes: “You heard my voice,” the man says, recalling his own plea that the LORD not hide his ear from his sighing and his cry. Arminian readers see God responding to the cry of the afflicted, and they note that the remembered answer strengthens present hope amid continuing distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s hearing as his faithful covenant response, which the man recalls to ground his present appeal. Readers differ on whether 3:56–61 looks back on an earlier rescue or speaks in confident anticipation; either way it moves the poem toward trust. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God hears the cry of his people.

verses.text: You came near in the day that I called on you. You said, “Don’t be afraid.”
verses.arminianNotes: “You came near in the day that I called on you.” Arminian readers treasure the nearness of God to the one who calls, and they hear in his answer, “Don’t be afraid,” the reassurance God gives his people throughout Scripture (compare Isaiah 41:10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God drawing near as his gracious initiative, answering the call he has prompted, and they hear the word against fear as resting on his presence rather than on changed circumstances. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as pastoral comfort for those in fear, spoken within the lament rather than after it.

verses.text: Lord, you have pleaded the causes of my soul. You have redeemed my life.
verses.arminianNotes: “Lord, you have pleaded the causes of my soul. You have redeemed my life.” Arminian readers see God as advocate and redeemer who takes up the cause of the oppressed (compare Jeremiah 50:34), and they hear the man’s confidence that his case rests in God’s hands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language of advocate and redeemer as God’s covenant commitment to his people, which many also hear fulfilled in Christ the advocate (compare 1 John 2:1). Shared ground: both traditions read “redeemed my life” first as rescue from death and enemies, and both see God as the one who vindicates the afflicted.

verses.text: LORD, you have seen my wrong. Judge my cause.
verses.arminianNotes: “LORD, you have seen my wrong. Judge my cause.” Arminian readers see the man bringing his case to the just Judge rather than seeking his own revenge, and they note that the wrong is one God has already seen, so the sufferer need not prove it before he prays.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal as resting on God’s righteous knowledge and his commitment to justice, so the man can wait for his verdict (compare Jeremiah 11:20). Shared ground: both traditions read 3:59 as the start of the closing plea for justice, offered to God and not carried out by the sufferer’s own hand.

verses.text: You have seen all their vengeance and all their plans against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have seen all their vengeance and all their plans against me.” Arminian readers stress that God knows the schemes of the wicked and that human plans against the righteous are fully visible to him, which encourages the sufferer to trust rather than retaliate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s complete knowledge of the enemies’ plans as part of his sovereign oversight, so their schemes cannot go beyond what he allows or finally escape his judgment. Shared ground: both traditions take comfort that God sees what the afflicted cannot fully expose or answer.

verses.text: You have heard their reproach, LORD, and all their plans against me,
verses.arminianNotes: “You have heard their reproach, LORD, and all their plans against me.” Arminian readers note the move from seeing to hearing: God attends to the words as well as the deeds of the enemies, so mocking speech against the afflicted is never lost on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition of “all their plans against me” (3:60–61) as emphasis on God’s full knowledge and his readiness to judge. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as confidence that reproach spoken against God’s people is heard by him, and both encourage the wronged to bring such words to God.

verses.text: the lips of those that rose up against me, and their plots against me all day long.
verses.arminianNotes: The man names “the lips of those that rose up against me, and their plots against me all day long.” Arminian readers see the constant hostility of his enemies, and they note that he lays it before God in detail rather than nursing it privately or repaying it himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the enemies’ words and plots as fully under God’s eye and therefore under his judgment, which frees the sufferer from the need to answer them himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as part of the case the afflicted man brings to the divine Judge.

verses.text: You see their sitting down and their rising up. I am their song.
verses.arminianNotes: “You see their sitting down and their rising up. I am their song.” Arminian readers hear God’s knowledge of the enemies’ whole lives (compare Psalm 139:2) and the man’s pain at being the subject of their mocking songs, as he said earlier (3:14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s complete awareness of his people’s enemies as assurance that he will act justly in his time. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as the sufferer entrusting the mockery to God, who sees every movement of those who oppose his people.

verses.text: You will pay them back, LORD, according to the work of their hands.
verses.arminianNotes: “You will pay them back, LORD, according to the work of their hands.” Arminian readers hear a plea for just recompense that matches judgment to deeds (compare Psalm 28:4), and they read it as a prayer for justice that leaves vengeance with God (compare Romans 12:19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the line as an appeal to God’s justice rather than private revenge, and they note that judgment according to deeds is a consistent biblical principle. Shared ground: both traditions read the imprecation soberly, as handing a wrong to God, and both set it beside Jesus’ command to pray for enemies (Matthew 5:44).

verses.text: You will give them hardness of heart, your curse to them.
verses.arminianNotes: “You will give them hardness of heart, your curse to them.” Arminian readers commonly read this hardening as judicial: God gives persistent oppressors over to the hardness they have chosen. The wider difference between the traditions on hardening is treated at Exodus 4:21 and Joshua 11:20.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly read the hardening as God’s sovereign judgment working through the enemies’ own will, without making him the author of their sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as a prayer for God’s just judgment on unrepentant oppressors, prayed soberly and not as a license for personal hatred.

verses.text: You will pursue them in anger, and destroy them from under the heavens of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The poem closes: “You will pursue them in anger, and destroy them from under the heavens of the LORD.” Arminian readers read the line as a plea for God’s final justice on unrepentant enemies, prayed by one who has himself been pursued (3:43, 3:52), and they leave it in God’s hands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the line as confidence that God will finally judge evil and vindicate his people, and they hear it within the larger hope of his just rule over all. Shared ground: both traditions receive the ending soberly, as a cry for justice from the depths of suffering, and neither treats it as permission for revenge.
